title: Loose Roman and tight Reformed definitions do not negate shared content
source_text: LIV. Itaque dum Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae ita laxam fidei definitionem tradunt, per id negare nolunt fidem vivam, quam tamen solam actu servare & justificare fatentur, esse assensum practicum atque efficacem, imo etiam includere divinae gratiae & misericordiae fiduciam. Et vice versa Doctores Reformati, dum fidem justificantem tam arcte definiunt, per id docere non intendunt ad naturam ejus nihil pertinere quod definitione ista non exprimatur, aut negare quod sit firmus assensus omnibus quae Verbo Dei continentur adhibitus, sed tali definitione istud solum exponere volunt quod fidei vivae atque justificantis maxime proprium esse existimant, & quod juxta ipsorum mentem illam a fide historica sive mortua potissimum distinguit atque disterminat.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore when the Doctors of the Roman Church hand down so loose a definition of faith, by that they do not mean to deny that living faith, which yet they confess alone actually saves and justifies, is a practical and efficacious assent, and even includes trust of divine grace and mercy. And conversely the Reformed Doctors, when they define justifying faith so narrowly, by that do not intend to teach that nothing belongs to its nature that is not expressed in that definition, or to deny that it is a firm assent given to all things contained in God Word, but by such a definition they want only to set out what they judge most proper to living and justifying faith, and what according to their mind chiefly distinguishes and bounds it from historic or dead faith.
pass_b_english: Rome loose definition does not deny living faith is practical efficacious assent including mercy-trust.
Reformed tight definitions do not deny firm assent to the whole Word; they spotlight what most distinguishes living justifying faith from historic dead faith.
